items.description: The four astronauts of NASA's Artemis II mission spent their fifth day in space Sunday testing the orange Orion Crew Survival System suits they would depend on in an emergency, as the spacecraft closed within roughly 60,000 miles of the Moon ahead of a historic flyby set for Monday afternoon.

items.title: Trump threatens to bomb Iran's infrastructure in Easter ultimatum

featured_image.name: Trump threatens Iran with "hell" if Hormuz strait isn't open in 48 hours

items.description: Global financial markets face a turbulent week after President Donald Trump used Easter Sunday to issue an expletive-laden ultimatum to Iran, threatening to destroy the country's power plants and bridges if it does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz by his April 7 deadline. The threats, combined with a stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report and a stark warning from the International Monetary Fund, have created a volatile cocktail of rising oil prices, falling equities, and dimming hopes for interest rate relief.

items.title: Russia's Ust-Luga port resumes crude loading after drone strikes

featured_image.name: Russia revises up oil export plans from Ust-Luga ...

items.description: Russia's key Baltic oil export hub at Ust-Luga resumed crude loading on Saturday after days of disruption caused by repeated Ukrainian drone strikes, according to Bloomberg News. The Aframax-class vessel The Jewel began cargo loading at the port, citing shipping data seen by Bloomberg, marking the first sign of recovery at a facility that had been largely shut down since late March.[1][2]

items.title: Trump delays Iran ultimatum again after US rescues downed airman

featured_image.name: On reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Trump tries to shift ...

items.description:
President Donald Trump issued an expletive-laden ultimatum to Iran on Sunday, threatening to strike the country's bridges and power plants unless Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz, hours after U.S. Special Operations forces successfully extracted the second crew member of an American fighter jet shot down over southern Iran.

The rescue and Trump's escalating rhetoric mark a turning point in the six-week-old conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran, which has engulfed Gulf states in a widening campaign of missile and drone strikes and triggered a global energy crisis.

items.title: Dar, Araghchi discuss de-escalation as Iran denies talks have stalled

items.description: Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar spoke by phone with Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi on Saturday to discuss the regional crisis, with Dar reaffirming Islamabad's commitment to de-escalation and the importance of resolving the conflict through dialogue, according to a Foreign Office statement. The two leaders agreed to maintain close contact as diplomatic efforts continue.[1][2]

items.description: Iranian drone and missile attacks struck civilian infrastructure across the Persian Gulf on Sunday, damaging a major petrochemical plant in Abu Dhabi, targeting a port in Sharjah, and setting fire to oil facilities in Kuwait, as Tehran's campaign of retaliation against Gulf states entered its sixth week.

items.description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi pushed back on Saturday against reports that Tehran had refused to participate in Pakistan-hosted peace talks, insisting that "we have never refused to go to Islamabad" and expressing gratitude for Pakistan's mediation efforts, even as the gap between Washington and Tehran's positions remains vast.

items.title: Trump says Putin has 'zero fear' of NATO in Easter tirade

featured_image.name: Trump says he's considering pulling U.S. out of 'paper tiger' NATO

items.description: President Donald Trump escalated his attacks on NATO on Easter Sunday, telling ABC News that his earlier calls for the alliance to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz were merely "a test" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin has "zero fear" of the military bloc. The remarks, made during phone calls from his Virginia golf club, mark the latest salvo in a week of increasingly hostile rhetoric toward America's closest allies.

Iran's military dismissed the warning and vowed that "the gates of hell" would open if the United States followed through on its threats.

items.title: Iran approves humanitarian passage as Hormuz yuan toll system takes shape

featured_image.name: Iran-US tensions: What would blocking Strait of Hormuz mean for oil ...

items.description:
Iran has extended an invitation to European, Asian, and Arab nations to negotiate formal transit agreements through the Strait of Hormuz, the latest escalation in a standoff that is reshaping how global oil moves and how it is paid for. The offer, announced this week by Head of the Government Information Council Elias Hazrati on Iranian state television, came as vessels already transiting the strait under Iranian escort are settling fees in Chinese yuan and stablecoins rather than U.S. dollars.[1][2]

"Iran fully controls the Strait of Hormuz," Hazrati said. "We will invite European, Asian and Arab countries that want to use it to conclude an agreement with us."[2]

items.title: Trump sets Tuesday 8 p.m. deadline for Iran on Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: Trump threatens to strike Iran's energy infrastructure if it does not open  Strait of Hormuz immediately | Stars and Stripes

items.description: President Donald Trump on Sunday issued his most explicit ultimatum yet to Iran, declaring in a Wall Street Journal interview that Tehran must reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Tuesday evening or face strikes on its power plants and bridges. He followed up with a cryptic post on Truth Social: "Tuesday, 8:00 P.M. Eastern Time!"[1][2][3]

items.title: Nations deploy rationing, tax cuts amid Iran war fuel crisis

featured_image.name: List of countries turning to four-day weeks as oil crisis bites

items.description: More than a month after the onset of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments across the globe are racing to deploy emergency measures to cushion their populations from surging energy costs and dwindling fuel supplies. The responses range from multibillion-euro spending packages in Europe to fuel rationing enforced by QR codes in Southeast Asia, underscoring the uneven toll of what the International Energy Agency has called the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market."[1][2]

items.description: As geopolitical turmoil in West Asia continues to ripple through global supply chains, governments in Egypt and India moved over the weekend to shore up reserves and crack down on disruptions to essential goods — each facing distinct but parallel pressures on food and fuel security.

items.description: Efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz through international diplomacy hit a wall this week as the United Nations Security Council postponed a vote on authorizing "defensive" force to protect shipping, while a UK-led coalition of more than 40 countries pledged to pursue economic and political pressure on Iran instead.

items.title: IEA warns Hormuz oil supply crunch could be largest in history

featured_image.name: Hormuz shipping disruptions raise risks for energy, fertilizers and ...

items.description:
More than five weeks after Iran effectively sealed the Strait of Hormuz to hostile shipping, the blockade has metastasized into the most severe supply chain crisis since the COVID-19 pandemic, sending oil prices to levels not seen since the 2008 financial crisis and threatening to tip the global economy into recession.

Brent crude spot prices surged to $141.36 per barrel in early April for immediate delivery, while WTI futures climbed past $112 after an 11% single-day jump on April 2. The International Energy Agency warned that the supply crunch will only intensify in the weeks ahead, calling the disruption potentially "the largest in history". United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby told ABC News that jet fuel costs have risen 70% since the war began, a burden now cascading through transportation, logistics, and consumer prices.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Iran exempts Iraq from Hormuz restrictions as weekly transits hit war-era high

featured_image.name: Why shadow tankers are the only ships still moving through the Strait of  Hormuz

items.description: Weekly vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz reached their highest level since the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel began on February 28, as an expanding roster of countries secures passage through the contested waterway. According to Lloyd's List Intelligence, 53 ships crossed the strait last week, up from 36 the previous week, though traffic remains more than 90% below pre-war levels.[1][2][3]

items.title: Israeli strikes kill at least 14 across Lebanon Sunday

featured_image.name: Lebanon says 13 killed in Israeli strike near Beirut hospital

items.description: Israeli airstrikes killed at least 14 people across Lebanon on Sunday, with one attack landing roughly 100 meters from Beirut's Rafik Hariri University Hospital — the country's largest public medical facility — as the five-week-old offensive showed no signs of easing and Hezbollah claimed its first cruise missile strike on an Israeli warship.
